newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan warns U.S. port row would hurt two-way ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan warns U.S. port row would hurt two-way ties.

text.p: Japan on Thursday strongly urged the United States to withdraw its threat of sanctions on Japanese shipping companies in a dispute over port practices and warned that the row could harm overall bilateral ties.
A government official said the two sides would meet to try to avert the sanctions, but added the dispute could prove tougher to settle than past U.S.-Japan trade rows.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said on Wednesday that it would slap $100,000 surcharges on Japanese vessels calling at U.S. ports in retaliation for what it termed "unfavourable restrictive practices". The commission added that the surcharges would become effective on April 14.

"The Transport Ministry can in no way accept the U.S. decision and will strongly urge the commission to withdraw it," Transport Minister Makoto Koga said in a statement, adding that Tokyo reserved the right to deal with the issue through multilateral and bilateral channels.

The FMC says that the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA), which is made up of port cargo-handling firms and mediates between labour unions and shipping companies, has put in place costly and restrictive practices that discriminate against foreign vessels.
The Commission said the JHTA exercises its control through a "prior consultation" system of negotiations and pre-approvals involving carriers, JHTA and waterfront unions.
The commission also said Japan's licensing requirements for terminal operators and stevedoring companies discriminated against foreign firms.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said on Thursday that Japan was discussing how to improve the "prior consultation system", which the United States and other nations want reformed.

"We cannot suppress our concern that the decision by the FMC might not only have a negative impact on Japan's efforts in this regard and delay a true solution of the problem, but also have a bad effect on overall Japan-U.S. ties," Ikeda said.
Japanese ship owners, meanwhile, lashed out at the FMC move, saying they were innocent of any wrongdoing.

"The U.S. decision is highly improper not only because there is a strong possibility that the measure could violate the U.S.-Japan Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation but also because the sanctions aimed at resolving port problems are directed at three innocent Japanese shipping firms," the Japanese Shipowners Association said in a statement.
"The sanctions, if imposed, would bring about grave economic damage on the three Japanese shipping companies and cannot be accepted," it added.

The FMC said the surcharge would be imposed each time a vessel owned or operated by Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd., Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd. and Nippon Yusen KK enters a U.S. port from abroad, but not from another U.S. port.

A Japanese government official said foreign and transport ministry officials would hold talks with their U.S. counterparts on the dispute, possibly as early as next week when transport officials will be in Washington for separate talks on civil aviation.

But he added that it would be difficult for Japan to come up with a new proposal quickly. "It would be hard to make a new proposal by next week, but through the end of March we need to get Japanese and foreign shipping companies together to consider what improvements can be made," he told Reuters.

Tokyo has made no decision on what steps it would take if Washington goes ahead with the planned sanctions, he said, adding that Japan might complain to the Geneva-based World Organisation (WTO) or seek bilateral consultations under the Japan-U.S. Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation.

Settling the row could be tough, given that neither the FMC nor the JHTA will take part in the government talks and that Japanese waterfront labour unions involved are "exceptionally strong" and have hefty political clout, he added.
